short_description: A casebook for law students on reasoning under uncertainty: priors, likelihood ratios, standards of proof as decision thresholds, the classic fallacies, and the statistics, economics and machines that now enter the courtroom, taught through leading English, American and comparative cases.
description:
Every trial is reasoning under uncertainty. A jury weighs a smear of DNA and a confused witness; a judge asks whether an insurer would have written a policy had it been told the truth. This book argues that the law is already Bayesian in its bones, and that saying so makes legal reasoning clearer, fairer and cheaper.
Written as a casebook for law students who have no statistics beyond school algebra, it teaches a reader to state a prior, compute a likelihood ratio, set a decision threshold from the costs of error, spot the fallacies, and explain each to a client, a jury and a judge. The first part builds the tools: odds and the weight of evidence, the island problem, Bayes factors, the prosecutor's and defence fallacies, standards of proof as decision rules, and the rules of evidence read through Bayes. The second reads English tort, damages, misrepresentation, contract, family law, the collapse of Greensill Capital and bankruptcy as constraints on belief and action. The third covers stories, graphical models of evidence and the pleadings game. The fourth follows Stephen Fienberg and Jay Kadane into the courtroom and then statistics in discrimination, securities, medical, intellectual property and digital evidence cases. The fifth compares common and civil law, legal origins and finance, Africa, the Indian courts and arbitration. The sixth studies order without the state. The last turns to the economics of Becker and Murphy, antitrust, litigation funding, sentencing and regulation, then to machine checked law in Lean and Catala, Lindley's challenge about machines that decide, explainable and fair algorithms, and a program for the law.
Chapters have leading cases and Notes and Questions; appendices give a probability toolkit, code for the main calculations, a table of cases, solutions, a glossary, a semester plan and a sample examination.

chapters.title: Why the Law Needs Bayes
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks why a court, which must both find facts and act on them, is best understood as a Bayesian decision maker. It sets out the three rules of probability (convexity, addition, multiplication), Bayes' rule in probability and odds form, the likelihood ratio or Bayes factor, and the expected loss threshold for conviction, with the Blackstone ratio of ten to one giving a posterior threshold of 10/11. It traces the history of probability in law from Jacob and Nicolas Bernoulli, Leibniz, Condorcet's jury theorem and Poisson's work on French juries, through Mill's hostility, Wigmore's charts, and Turing and Good's weight of evidence, to the Finkelstein and Fairley proposal and Tribe's Trial by Mathematics. It presents Lindley's challenge that a court is a computation combining probabilities and utilities, and answers objections such as the presumption of innocence, single event probabilities, and juries that cannot do arithmetic, using R v Adams as an illustration. It then previews the economics of courts, legal AI, formal verification in Lean and Catala, comparative common and civil law reasoning, legal origins, and order without the state. The chapter argues that decision theory under uncertainty has one coherent form and that it fits the law.

chapters.title: Bayesian Decisions for Lawyers
chapters.summary:
This chapter presents Bayesian decision theory for lawyers as four questions: what are the actions, what are the states of the world, what is each consequence worth, and how probable is each state given the evidence. It builds the loss table for a criminal verdict with false conviction loss c_I and false acquittal loss c_II, and connects it to the classical language of Type I and Type II errors, significance level, power, and the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. It derives the Bayes risk of a decision rule, shows that the optimal error rate depends on the base rate and the loss ratio rather than a fixed five per cent, and shows that the posterior threshold rule applied case by case minimises aggregate risk. A worked example shows how a one per cent false positive rate can still give about one innocent person in twenty three among positive results. The chapter extends the framework to many actions, continuous decisions and damages (posterior mean under squared error, posterior median under absolute error, asymmetric loss and quantiles), sequential decisions, the costs of process and the value of accuracy, and deterrence and incentives. Worked examples cover bail decisions and the choice whether to sue under the American rule, the English costs rule (CPR 44.2) and qualified one way costs shifting.

chapters.title: Odds, Likelihood and the Weight of Evidence
chapters.summary:
This chapter develops the likelihood ratio as the currency of evidence and applies it to statistical errors in criminal trials. It explains why the likelihood ratio is comparative, separates the expert from the fact finder, and multiplies for independent items so that Good's weight of evidence in decibans adds. It works through the prosecutor's fallacy and the island problem formula, the defence fallacy, the independence fallacy in People v Collins, and the Sally Clark case, where the correct comparison is between double murder and double sudden infant death. It reworks R v Adams, in which Peter Donnelly presented Bayes' theorem to the jury and the Court of Appeal was hostile, and covers R v Doheny and Adams on the presentation of DNA evidence, and R v T on footwear marks and the limits of likelihood ratios. Further sections read relevance (DPP v Kilbourne, Federal Rule of Evidence 401) as a likelihood ratio, read Re B (Children) on the binary standard of proof, treat a trial as a sequential probability ratio test in the manner of Turing and Wald, discuss verbal scales such as that of ENFSI, the cab problem and base rate neglect, and the blue bus case Smith v Rapid Transit on naked statistics.

chapters.title: Classic Problems: Simpson, the Island and the Search
chapters.summary:
This chapter works three classic problems and the graphical tools that extend them. The first is the argument of Alan Dershowitz in the O. J. Simpson trial that prior domestic violence was nearly irrelevant because fewer than one battered woman in 2,500 is killed by her partner in a year. Following I. J. Good, the chapter shows that the relevant quantity conditions on the murder as well, and on the stated numbers gives a probability of about eight ninths, and it names the error the Dershowitz fallacy. It also discusses the criminal and civil verdicts in Simpson and the defence attack on laboratory contamination. The second problem is the island problem, treated coherently by Dawid and Mortera, with uncertainty about the match probability (the size biased mean), search strategies in which excluded inhabitants strengthen the case, and relatives. The third is how a suspect was found, including database searches and the dispute between Balding and Donnelly and the National Research Council report. The chapter then presents Jim Smith's event trees and chain event graphs, activity level propositions, object oriented Bayesian networks for forensic genetics, and the 2024 comparison of Wigmore charts, Bayesian networks and chain event graphs on the Kercher case.

chapters.title: Bayes Factors in the Courtroom
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks how a Bayes factor works when the competing legal propositions are composite, that is, families of distributions with unknown parameters, as they are for DNA profiles with laboratory error, low template DNA and secondary transfer, and for statistical evidence in discrimination cases. It also treats composite theories as mixtures over subplots, the Bayesian Occam factor and The Popi M, and it ends with principles for communicating Bayes factors to a fact finder. It shows that laboratory error can cap the weight of a DNA match, and that the two sides of the database debate answer different questions.

chapters.title: Fallacies of Classical Inference
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks which misreadings of classical statistics recur in litigation and what a Bayesian analysis of the same data would conclude. It builds on Finkelstein and Levin's Statistics for Lawyers and sets out ten fallacies, each with a statement, an explanation and a worked example: reading the p value as the probability that the null is true, treating non significance as no effect, equating significance with importance, misreading confidence intervals as probability statements, ignoring multiple comparisons (the Texas sharpshooter), the dependence of p values on the stopping rule and the likelihood principle, the two or three standard deviations rule of Castaneda and Hazelwood, one tailed versus two tailed tests, combining p values (Fisher's method, Lucia de Berk), and testing without an alternative (People v Collins). The cases include Matrixx Initiatives v Siracusano and Milward v Acuity. It argues that the absence of an explicit prior is what produces the fallacies, and that the remedy is to state the prior and show how the conclusion depends on it. The worked examples are constructed to be realistic, and some follow the pattern of decided cases.

chapters.title: Standards of Proof as Decision Rules
chapters.summary:

It then turns to Lindley's graduated sanctions, the value of information and when a court should stop and decide, the conjunction paradox of Cohen against element by element proof, relative plausibility, and Scotland's not proven verdict and its abolition. It argues that the paradoxes reflect the all or nothing form of the law more than a failure of probability.

chapters.title: The Law of Evidence Through Bayes

The chapter argues that these rules can be understood as tools for managing uncertain likelihood ratios, and that each trades accuracy against other values.

chapters.title: Bayesian Interpretations of English Tort Law
chapters.summary:
Does English negligence law have a Bayesian structure? The chapter reads the reasonable person as a Bayesian agent whose beliefs and precautions are judged against the evidence available. It works through breach (probability, severity, cost of precaution and social value in Bolton v Stone, Paris v Stepney, Latimer v AEC and Watt v Hertfordshire), the Hand formula B less than PL, professional standards (Bolam), and informed consent as an expected utility or value of information test (Montgomery). It then treats causation: the but for test, the doubling of risk rule for epidemiological evidence (Sienkiewicz), material contribution and the Fairchild exception for mesothelioma, and loss of a chance (Hotson, Gregg v Scott). It also covers remoteness (Wagon Mound), duty of care (Donoghue v Stevenson, Caparo), contributory negligence and strict liability (Rylands v Fletcher). The chapter argues that foreseeability is a probability judgment, that causation is a counterfactual probability, and that proportional recovery for lost chances is the Bayesian answer to Lord Hoffmann's deterministic view. Exercises include a gamma Poisson analysis of Bolton v Stone and a Fairchild apportionment calculation.

chapters.title: Mass Torts and Scientific Causation
chapters.summary:

chapters.title: Assessing Damages Under Uncertainty
chapters.summary:
How should a court turn uncertain evidence into a sum of money? The chapter treats an award as a number drawn from a predictive distribution and asks which summary of it the compensatory principle requires. It covers future losses and lump sums (Wells v Wells on discount rates, the Ogden tables, contingencies, and periodical payments under the Damages Act 1996, Thompstone), lost profits and the American reasonable certainty rule (Story Parchment), loss of a chance in contract (Chaplin v Hicks), and presumptions that resolve uncertainty against the wrongdoer (Armory v Delamirie), read as a choice of posterior quantile. It discusses negotiating damages (Morris-Garner v One Step, Sempra Metals), hindsight in assessment (The Golden Victory), combining expert estimates, interest and the time value of money, and the use of data in damages. The chapter argues that liability is judged on the information at the time of the act while quantum may use later information, and it returns to this in the bankruptcy chapter.

chapters.title: Children, Families and Decisions About Risk
chapters.summary:
How do family courts decide under uncertainty about past events and future risk to children? chapters.title: The Greensill Case
chapters.summary:
What does the collapse of Greensill Capital show about reliance, representations and information? The chapter uses supply chain finance (reverse factoring) as a case study, with the Credit Suisse funds, trade credit insurance, GFG Alliance, SoftBank and Katerra, and relies on public statements, official reports and judgments rather than contested allegations. It models the chain of beliefs from obligors to investors as a sequence of channels where information is lost, concentration and tail risk in a simulated loss distribution, future receivables as a different hypothesis from existing receivables, Beta posterior updating on late and rolled over payments, and a Bayesian network showing that insurance written on the originator's presentation is not an independent signal. It asks the insurance questions under fair presentation, discusses directors' disqualification and lobbying as value of information, and measures loss and causation. It draws four lessons: chains weaken information, tails matter, dependent signals should not be added, and remedies should be counterfactual and proportional.

chapters.title: Bankruptcy, Solvency and Hindsight
chapters.summary:
How should courts judge solvency after a firm has failed, without hindsight? The chapter treats the balance sheet, unreasonably small capital and ability to pay tests of fraudulent transfer law as three posteriors, following Heaton's reading through financial economics. chapters.title: Bayesian Stories
chapters.summary:
Does storytelling in the courtroom conflict with probabilistic reasoning, and how can a narrative be scored as evidence? The chapter argues that a story is a generative model of how the evidence arose, so that comparing stories is Bayesian model comparison. The three criteria of the Pennington and Hastie story model, coverage, coherence and uniqueness, are mapped to the likelihood, the prior and the concentration of the posterior, and the integral over a story's free parameters supplies a Bayesian Occam's razor against flexible stories. Weight of evidence is measured in decibans, and the posterior probability of guilt is written as a sum over all guilty and innocent stories, which shows why comparing only the two stories the parties tell can mislead, as in Lord Brandon's remark in The Popi M. It then works through the murder of Meredith Kercher in Perugia (Amanda Knox, Raffaele Sollecito, Rudy Guede): the lone assailant story against the joint story, illustrative decibans for each item of evidence (DNA on the knife and the bra clasp, the absence of Knox traces, the broken window, the statements), a prior, and a posterior range. The authors present the numbers as illustrations, not findings. The chapter argues that the case turned on the probability of DNA contamination, and it closes with the use of large language models to generate and score stories.

chapters.title: Graphical Models of Evidence
chapters.summary:
How can the structure of a body of legal evidence be drawn and computed with? The chapter moves from Wigmore charts to Bayesian networks, directed acyclic graphs with conditional probability tables, and explains the three elementary structures (chain, fork and collider), conditional independence, d separation and explaining away. It presents Kadane and Schum's probabilistic analysis of the Sacco and Vanzetti evidence (Commonwealth v Sacco and Vanzetti), including Bullet III, the ballistic comparison, the substitution defence and consciousness of guilt evidence, with a simplified network. It describes the idioms of Fenton, Neil and Lagnado (evidence and accuracy, cause and consequence, alternative explanation, opportunity and motive, witness dependence) and object oriented Bayesian networks. It then applies causal graphs and Pearl's structural causal models to tort causation: the but for test as a counterfactual computed by abduction, action and prediction on a twin network, overdetermination, the NESS test, and material contribution in mesothelioma cases such as Fairchild read as a collider problem. It closes by arguing that graphs are choices that reflect a theory of the case, which makes them contestable, and by comparing Wigmore charts, Bayesian networks and chain event graphs on the Kercher evidence. Exercises compute explaining away and the effect of witness collusion on a likelihood ratio.

chapters.title: The Pleadings Game and Generative Bayesian Computation
chapters.summary:
How can pleadings, issue formation and the plausibility standard be modelled probabilistically, and can a neural network be trained to assess a pleaded claim? The chapter starts from Thomas Gordon's Pleadings Game, a dialogue game that turns assertions, denials and defeasible arguments into a set of issues, and adds probabilities by treating each issue as resolved for the claimant or the defendant and the claim as succeeding when the issues satisfy the elements of the cause of action. It reads the US plausibility standard of Bell Atlantic v Twombly and Ashcroft v Iqbal, in contrast with Conley v Gibson, as an implicit posterior threshold, and justifies a threshold by the cost of discovery, p greater than c over V. It compares English strike out and summary judgment under the Civil Procedure Rules (Swain v Hillman, Three Rivers District Council v Bank of England (No 3)). The central method is generative Bayesian computation: simulate disputes from a generative model, train a quantile neural network on parameter and data pairs, and obtain posterior quantiles for a new case by amortised, likelihood free inference. A Hedley Byrne negligent misstatement example illustrates the pleading exchange, and the chapter discusses case law as training data, selection bias, and the limits of a machine that cannot decide what the law is.

chapters.title: Pleadings in Practice: Worked Cases
chapters.summary:
How does the Bayesian pleadings analysis work on concrete claims, and what step does it indicate? The chapter gives a six step recipe (list the elements, map the pleadings, assign issue probabilities, handle dependence, compute the probability of success and expected recovery, compare the expected value of continuing with the alternatives) and applies it to five illustrative cases. Product negligence, after Donoghue v Stevenson, combines duty, breach and causation with positive correlation and ends in settlement. An exclusion clause, after Photo Production v Securicor, shows that uncertainty about the law must be priced and makes an appeal on a point of law the indicated step. A negligent misstatement by an investment adviser, after Hedley Byrne and Manchester Building Society v Grant Thornton, multiplies falsity, breach and scope of duty and points to mediation. Age discrimination pleading, after Swierkiewicz v Sorema, Twombly and Iqbal, multiplies likelihood ratios for the replacement, the reviews and the remarks. A price fixing complaint after Twombly shows how parallel conduct, the lack of a cost explanation and an industry meeting move the posterior, with the outcome depending on the plausibility threshold and on plus factors. A table collects the decisions, and the chapter ends by explaining how a network could be trained on such labelled cases. The numbers are illustrative.

chapters.title: Fienberg and the Evolving Role of Statistics in the Courts
chapters.summary:
What did Stephen Fienberg show about the use of statistics in courts and public decisions? The chapter surveys his work: the 1989 National Research Council report The Evolving Role of Statistical Assessments as Evidence in the Courts and its six findings; a model of the adversarial expert in which each party calls the most favourable of k experts, so the court sees order statistics that exaggerate real uncertainty, with the English remedies of the duty to the court, the single joint expert and concurrent evidence under the Civil Procedure Rules; and the misreading of significance tests. Castaneda v Partida (1977) and the two or three standard deviation rule are analysed with a Bayes factor and Lindley's paradox, together with Hazelwood and the choice of the relevant population, and Duren v Missouri on the fair cross section, absolute and comparative disparity. The chapter also covers his analysis of the 1969 draft lottery, the census adjustment dispute (Anderson and Fienberg, Department of Commerce v House of Representatives), the 2003 National Research Council report on the polygraph with its base rate argument for screening, and Fienberg and Kadane's 1983 advice that experts present likelihoods or Bayes factors and a range of priors, not a posterior probability of guilt.

chapters.title: Kadane on Skill, Chance and the Expert Witness
chapters.summary:
How should courts measure skill and chance, and what does a Bayesian expert witness do? The chapter follows Joseph Kadane's work as a consultant and expert. It then surveys his other engagements: jury challenges (Azania v State), peremptory strikes and Batson v Kentucky, driving while black and State v Soto with missing data, hierarchical models for employment discrimination and Wal Mart v Dukes, and sampling in tax audits. It closes with four lessons for expert witnesses: define the question in the law's terms, use simple and robust models, be open about the prior, and accept that courts may decide on other grounds.

chapters.title: Discrimination, Regression and the Burden of Proof

chapters.title: Securities Fraud, Event Studies and Prices as Evidence

chapters.title: Clusters, Coincidence and Medical Murder Cases
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks what a cluster of deaths around a nurse or doctor proves, and how statistics have both convicted the guilty and contributed to miscarriages of justice. Its cases are Lucia de Berk, where the one in three hundred and forty two million figure of Elffers was later discredited, Lucy Letby, Beverley Allitt and Harold Shipman. chapters.title: Legal Origins and Finance
chapters.summary:
This chapter presents the legal origins thesis of La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny (1997, 1998) that countries whose law descends from English common law protect investors more strongly than those with French, German or Scandinavian civil law, and that stronger protection goes with larger stock markets, more initial public offerings and more dispersed ownership. It explains how investor protection was measured: the antidirector rights index, creditor rights, and enforcement measures. It covers the 2008 survey on legal origin as a style of social control, the Courts paper on procedural formalism (Djankov and coauthors, 2003), and Glaeser and Shleifer's history of why origins differ. It then sets out the critics: Spamann's recoding of the index, the identification problem and colonial history (Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson; Klerman and coauthors), the great reversals of Rajan and Zingales, and Roe's politics account. A Bayesian assessment uses model averaging, measurement error models and hierarchical shrinkage across legal families, and concludes that rules matter but origin is a weaker and confounded explanation.

chapters.title: Africa as a Natural Experiment
chapters.summary:
This chapter treats Africa as a natural laboratory for the legal origins thesis, since colonial powers transplanted common law, French civil law, Roman Dutch law and other systems, alongside Islamic and customary law. It explains why law cannot be separated from the rest of the colonial package, and uses border designs and regression discontinuity (Michalopoulos and Papaioannou on partitioned ethnic homelands) to isolate colonial effects. Cameroon, a bijural state divided between British and French mandates, is the sharpest case (Lee and Schultz 2012). The chapter proposes a hierarchical Bayesian border model with Gaussian process smooth terms and border level covariates. It then discusses OHADA harmonised business law and its Common Court of Justice and Arbitration, the Anglophone crisis and the lawyers' strike of 2016, customary law and the repugnancy clause as an evidence problem, annulment of presidential elections by the Supreme Court of Kenya (2017) and the Constitutional Court of Malawi (2020), and how slow courts affect contracts and development.

chapters.title: The Indian Court System
chapters.summary:
This chapter describes the Indian court system and argues that delay is a decision problem. It opens with the scale of pendency reported through the National Judicial Data Grid, then covers the structure of the Supreme Court (Articles 32, 124, 136 and 142), the High Courts (Articles 226 and 227), public interest litigation (Hussainara Khatoon 1979, Article 21 and speedy trial), and Lok Adalats under the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987. It reads Vivekananda's definition of law and the Nyaya idea of vyapti as a theory of induction. It discusses the Indian Evidence Act 1872 of James Fitzjames Stephen, section 3 on proof as belief or prudent action and section 114 presumptions, and the replacement statutes of 2023 (Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam). A queueing model with Little's law, the c mu rule and Gittins index for Bayesian triage, value of information, adjournments, eCourts, artificial intelligence and bail as expected utility (State of Rajasthan v Balchand, bail not jail) follow.

chapters.title: Arbitration, Mediation and Private Adjudication
chapters.summary:
This chapter applies the book's decision framework to private adjudication and to the choice of forum. It explains why commercial parties arbitrate (neutrality, expertise, confidentiality, finality, enforceability under the New York Convention 1958) in terms of accuracy, cost of delay and the value of appeals. chapters.title: Vendetta, Honour and the Mafia
chapters.summary:
This chapter examines order without effective state courts through two bodies of work. Roger Gould studied vendetta in nineteenth century Corsica using French court records and found that revenge was rare and was a targeted sanction against collective aggression, a display of solidarity, not blind collective responsibility. Gould's Collision of Wills (2003) argues that conflict is most likely where social rank is ambiguous, which the chapter reads as disagreement about a posterior, alongside Priest and Klein on litigation and Fearon on war. Diego Gambetta analysed the Sicilian mafia as an industry selling private protection, with reputation and costly signals as its capital, and economists have tested origins in land fragmentation, sulphur and citrus exports. The chapter covers Article 416 bis, Tommaso Buscetta and Giovanni Falcone, the maxi trial in Palermo, omerta, pentiti, and the weight of accomplice testimony under Article 192 of the Italian code of criminal procedure and the Marino judgment (1992), with likelihood ratios and corroboration. It ends with network inference and lessons for law.

chapters.title: Costs, Expected Utility and Deterrence
chapters.summary:
This chapter applies expected utility theory to crime, punishment and the courts themselves. It sets out Becker's economic approach to crime and punishment: a potential offender offends if the expected gain exceeds the probability of conviction times the sanction, and the state chooses enforcement spending and sanctions to minimise the sum of the harm from crime and the costs of enforcement. It covers optimal fines and the probability and severity trade off, enforcers' incentives and corruption, the market for illegal goods, rational addiction, social interactions in crime, the value of a statistical life, and punitive damages and the multiplier. It then turns to the economics of litigation and settlement: why cases settle, the Priest and Klein selection of disputes for litigation, asymmetric information, who pays the costs (the English and American rules), plea bargaining, and the cost of the courts. Cases discussed include State Farm v Campbell and Twombly. Readers searching for deterrence theory, law and economics, optimal enforcement, punitive damages ratios, settlement models or plea bargaining models will find the chapter's argument and its sources here.

chapters.title: Antitrust Under Uncertainty
chapters.summary:
This chapter treats antitrust as decision making under uncertainty about future harm. It begins with predicting harm and with error costs (false positives and false negatives) in enforcement, and discusses the debate over error cost analysis. chapters.title: Judges, Costs and the Justice System
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks what the justice system costs and how its scarce resources should be allocated. It starts from the idea that justice is a scarce resource, and then examines the value of accuracy in adjudication (Kaplow's question, the trade off between accuracy and cost, and accuracy about what). It treats the docket as a portfolio, judges as a cost of the system, and the cost of delay. It discusses appeals as error correction, rules on who pays costs (the English and American rules, proportionality and costs management, legal aid), the measurement of system performance, and judges as decision makers. The method is decision theoretic: the benefit of additional accuracy is weighed against the resources it consumes, and the same reasoning is applied to allocating judges' time and to designing appeals. Readers searching for law and economics of procedure, court congestion, case management, fee shifting, costs budgeting, legal aid funding, or error correction in appeals will find the chapter's argument and its sources here.

chapters.title: Litigation Funding, Class Actions and Claims as Assets
chapters.summary:
This chapter treats legal claims as risky assets and applies decision theory to their valuation, funding and aggregation. Bates v Post Office appears as an example of group litigation and funding. chapters.title: Sentencing, Bail and Parole as Decisions
chapters.summary:
This chapter treats sentencing, bail and parole as decisions under uncertainty that follow the verdict. It sets out the objectives of sentencing (deterrence, incapacitation, retribution and rehabilitation), guidelines as decision rules (the Sentencing Council guidelines in England and Wales and the federal guidelines after Booker), and bail, framed as a decision with Type I and Type II errors, together with reform. chapters.title: Verification: Lean, Catala and Machine Checked Law
chapters.summary:
Can formal verification check the logical and arithmetical steps of legal decisions? The chapter treats a judgment as an argument from findings of fact and law to an order, and asks which steps a proof assistant such as Lean can certify. It introduces Lean and its kernel, writes the Hand formula in the Carroll Towing example and a conjunction of the elements of a negligence claim as short theorems, and reviews rules as code: the Prolog encoding of the British Nationality Act 1981, Lawsky's default logic for tax statutes, and the Catala language. It then verifies Bayes factor computations such as the island problem, with interval certificates for ranges of a contamination rate, and treats defeasibility and burden of proof. It argues that facts, open texture and discretion with values cannot be verified, and that autoformalisation errors become hidden premises, citing the Dutch childcare benefits scandal and the Post Office Horizon cases. It ends with three proposals: publish statutory computations as code, attach checkable specifications to forensic likelihood ratios, and use structural checks on trial findings on appeal.

chapters.title: Should Machines Decide? Lindley's Challenge
chapters.summary:
Should machines decide, and how should courts use artificial intelligence? The chapter restates Lindley's challenge: if a court combines probabilities and utilities coherently, that task is a computation. It surveys what machines already do: actuarial risk assessment and State v Loomis, prediction of decisions (Aletras and colleagues, Katz, Bommarito and Blackman), technology assisted review in Da Silva Moore v Publicis Groupe and Pyrrho Investments v MWB Property, hallucinated citations in Mata v Avianca and Ayinde v Haringey, and online courts. It then describes ten channels of change: triage, drafting, evidence analysis, deepfakes and the likelihood ratio of recordings, settlement under the Priest and Klein model, decision support, consistency and noise, access to justice, verification, and the role of the judge. It treats fairness and calibration, including the impossibility results of Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan and Chouldechova, the COMPAS dispute, and the selective labels problem, and closes with eight requirements for a Bayesian machine in court.

chapters.title: Verifying AI, Explaining AI and the Ethics of Legal Machines

chapters.title: Intuition, Miracles and the Limits of Human Judgment
chapters.summary:
How should a fact finder weigh testimony and opinion, and how reliable is human intuition? The chapter begins with Hume on miracles in the Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748) and reads his maxim as a statement about posterior odds: testimony establishes an extraordinary event only if its falsehood would be more improbable than the event. It discusses Earman's criticism, that Hume neglected independent witnesses, and applies the maxim to serious allegations, linking it to Lord Nicholls in Re H and to the medical murder cases. It then reviews heuristics and biases (Tversky and Kahneman), anchoring among judges (Englich, Mussweiler and Strack), the conditions under which intuition works (Kahneman and Klein), Meehl on clinical versus statistical prediction, Dawes on improper linear models, and the Kleinberg bail study. It states Lindley's point about coherence and ends with a six step procedure for weighing testimony using priors, likelihood ratios, shared sources and thresholds.

chapters.title: A Bayesian Program for the Law
chapters.summary:
What would a Bayesian program for the law look like in practice? This concluding chapter gathers the book's argument into ten proposals, each tied to earlier chapters: report likelihood ratios with ranges, direct juries on conditioning with the island problem and the Simpson argument, separate activity from source, proportionate remedies where causation is probabilistic (lost chances, clinical negligence, the Insurance Act 2015), judge investment representations by their implied distributions as in Greensill, combine market and expert evidence of solvency in fraudulent transfer and wrongful trading cases, use single joint experts who report distributions, triage by expected cost of delay, publish law as code where it is computation, and hold machine tools to Bayesian standards. It revisits objections to Bayesian legal reasoning, including the presumption of innocence as a prior of one over N and the view that law is a human practice, and closes on Lindley's expectation that all would be Bayesian by 2020.

chapters.title: The Future and Promise of AI in Law
chapters.summary:
What will AI change in law, what can it promise, and what can it not? The chapter predicts five changes: legal information becomes cheap, prediction becomes explicit, disputes are selected differently as better prediction raises settlement (Priest and Klein), evidence changes through deepfakes and algorithmic decisions that become evidence, and overloaded courts triage. It lists what AI can promise: consistency against noise, coherence in updating and thresholds (Lindley's challenge), access to justice, citing the California 2024 Justice Gap Study, and verification in which machines draft, verifiers check and people judge. It lists what AI cannot promise: choosing values, handling facts absent from its data, and legitimacy, which depends on accountable persons and fair process. It closes with what a lawyer of the future should know, arguing that understanding likelihood ratios and calibration will be part of competence.

chapters.title: A Probability Toolkit for Lawyers
chapters.summary:
This appendix is a short self contained primer on the probability the book uses, written for readers with no statistics. It states the three rules of probability, Bayes' rule in probability and odds form, and independence and conditional independence. It then covers evidence: the likelihood ratio and weight of evidence, composite hypotheses, the island formula for a match when the source may be someone else in a population, uncertain match probabilities, and beta binomial prediction. A section on decisions gives expected utility, the decision threshold that follows from the losses of the two kinds of error, and the value of information. Short sections on the binomial, Poisson, beta, gamma and normal distributions, a list of named fallacies (prosecutor's fallacy, defence fallacy, Dershowitz fallacy, independence fallacy, base rate neglect, double counting, hindsight bias, selection neglect) and a note on graphical models and Bayesian networks, including blocking and colliders, close it. A reader uses it as a reference to look up a rule or definition when a chapter relies on it.

chapters.title: Solutions to Selected Questions
chapters.summary:
This appendix gives worked answers to the computational questions at the ends of the chapters, and brief guidance on some of the discussion questions, organised chapter by chapter. Numbers are rounded and for some questions only part of the question is answered. The answers use the tools of the book: decision thresholds and the ratio of losses they imply, binomial calculations such as the probability that a jury of twelve reaches a correct verdict, posterior odds from likelihood ratios, the island formula, and Bayes factors. The first solutions show, for example, that a threshold of 0.95 implies a loss ratio of 19 and a threshold of one half implies equal losses. The third shows that, with a uniform prior over one million people and a feature shared by one in a thousand, the posterior that a matching suspect is the offender is about 0.001. chapters.title: Using This Book in a Course
chapters.summary:
This appendix suggests how to teach from the book. It proposes three paths: a fifteen week law school seminar on evidence and probability, given as a week by week schedule that pairs chapters with leading cases such as Collins, Clark, Adams, Matrixx, Re B, Turnbull, Hanson, Daubert, Gregg v Scott, Fairchild, Wells v Wells and Twombly; a course for statisticians and economists that emphasises models and computation, Bayes factors, graphical models and generative Bayesian computation; and a two day short course for judges, prosecutors and practitioners built from selected chapters on odds, the island problem, standards of proof, evidence, clusters, intuition and machines. chapters.title: A Sample Examination
chapters.summary:
This appendix gives a sample three hour examination for a law school course built on the book, with notes on what a strong answer contains. The questions are original and the facts invented. Question 1 concerns a courier charged with importing drugs, and asks students to state the propositions, estimate likelihood ratios for four items of evidence, identify items that are not conditionally independent, compute a posterior and draft a jury direction on nervousness. Question 2 concerns a delayed diagnosis of a heart attack and asks for advice under English law with reference to Barnett, Hotson and Gregg v Scott, the probability of causation computed from risks of sixty and thirty five per cent, the French approach of loss of a chance, and proportional recovery. Question 3 concerns a machine learning tool predicting failure to appear, and asks about calibration, group fairness, the selective labels problem and the implied loss ratio of a twenty per cent threshold. Students use it to practise and instructors to set papers.
